gaps.sentence: There's ___ at the door — go and see who it is.
gaps.explanation: 'Somebody' is used in affirmative sentences for an unknown person; 'anybody' belongs to questions and negatives.

gaps.sentence: The lecture was ___ attended than the organisers had hoped.
gaps.explanation: 'Well attended' compares with the adverb: less well attended.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the students has been given a personal timetable.
gaps.hint: this is the only option that can be followed by 'of' and take a singular verb
gaps.explanation: 'Each of the students has ...' is correct; 'every' cannot take 'of' here and 'all/both' need a plural verb.

gaps.sentence: You can park on ___ side of the street.
gaps.hint: singular noun meaning 'this one or that one'
gaps.explanation: 'Either side' means one side or the other (both are allowed); 'both' would need the plural 'sides'.

gaps.sentence: There is ___ use asking him — he never checks his messages.
gaps.explanation: 'There is no use doing something' = it is pointless.

gaps.sentence: We can take the ferry or the tunnel — ___ way takes about three hours.
gaps.hint: one of two options, singular noun
gaps.explanation: 'Either way' means whichever of the two you choose; 'both' would need 'ways'.

gaps.sentence: I don't like this colour — do you have it in ___ colours?
gaps.explanation: 'Other colours' uses 'other' as an adjective before the plural noun; 'another' is followed by singular nouns.

gaps.sentence: We had ___ luggage that the taxi couldn't take it all.
gaps.explanation: 'So much luggage that …' — luggage is uncountable.
